topic.name: The Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation

question.text: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w) \to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that \[ u = 2x + y,\qquad v = -x + 3y -2z, \qquad w = 3y + 4z. \]
question.explanation:
For a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\w\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w)\\y(u,v,w)\\z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

In this case, we're only given $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ as follows:

  • First, we compute $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ using the relation \[ \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1}. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} &= 2 &\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} &= 1 &\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} &= 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} &= -1 &\quad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} &= 3 &\quad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} &= -2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} &= 0 &\quad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} &= 3 &\quad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} &= 4 \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} &= \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} &\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 2 \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} -1 \begin{vmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=2(12+6) - 1(-4-0) \\[5pt] &= 40. \end{align*}

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{40}. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w) \to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that \[ u = 3x + yz,\qquad v = z, \qquad w = -y. \]
question.explanation:
For a transformation \[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\w\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w)\\y(u,v,w)\\z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

In this case, we're only given $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ as follows:

  • First, we compute $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ using the relation \[ \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1}. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} &= 3 &\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} &= z &\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} &= y \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} &= 0 &\quad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} &= 0 &\quad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} &= 1\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} &= 0 &\quad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} &= -1 &\quad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} &= 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} &= \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} &\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & z & y \\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 3 \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = 3(0+1) \\[5pt] & = 3 \end{align*}

Finally, we take the reciprocal: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{align*}

question.text:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf T$ is defined as

\[ \mathbf T: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ w \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} e^{u}+v \\ v+w \\ vw \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.choice1: The critical points lie on the plane $v=w.$
question.choice2: The critical points lie on the $vw-$plane.
question.choice3: The critical points lie on the $uv-$plane.
question.choice4: The critical points lie on the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=4.$
question.choice5: The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v=2w^2.$
question.explanation:
For a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\w\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w)\\y(u,v,w)\\z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have

\[ x(u,v,w) = e^{u}+v, \qquad y(u,v,w) = v+w, \qquad z(u,v,w) = vw. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= e^{u} & \quad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= 1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} &= 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 0 & \quad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} &= 0 & \quad \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} &= w & \quad \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} &= v \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= \begin{vmatrix} e^u & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & w & v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= e^u \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ w & v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= e^{u}(v-w). \end{align*}

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} =0.$ So, we obtain

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= 0 \\[5pt] e^{u}(v-w) &= 0 \\[5pt] v-w &= 0. \end{align*}

The equation $v-w = 0$ defines the plane $v=w.$

example.title: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation

question.text:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf T$ is defined as

\[ \mathbf T: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ w \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u+2w \\ v-u \\ uw \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.choice1: The critical points lie on the plane $u=2w.$
question.choice2: The critical points lie on the plane $u+v-2w=0.$
question.choice3: The critical points lie on the $vw-$ plane.
question.choice4: The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v=u^2.$
question.choice5: The critical points lie on the elliptic cylinder $u^2+2w^2=1.$
question.explanation:
For a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\w\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w)\\y(u,v,w)\\z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have

\[ x(u,v,w) = u+2w, \qquad y(u,v,w) = v-u, \qquad z(u,v,w) = uw. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= 1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &=0 & \quad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} &= 2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= -1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} &= 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} &= w & \quad \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} &= 0 & \quad \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} &= u \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2\\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ w & 0 & u \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0 & u \end{vmatrix} + 2\begin{vmatrix} -1 &1\\ w & 0 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] &= 1(u-0) + 2(0-w) \\[5pt] &= u-2w. \end{align*}

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} =0.$ So, we obtain

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= 0 \\[5pt] u-2w&= 0. \end{align*}

The equation $u - 2w = 0$ defines the plane $u=2w.$

example.title: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation

question.text:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf T$ is defined as

\[ \mathbf T: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ w \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u+3w \\ v+2w \\ v^2-u \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.choice1: The critical points lie on the plane $v=\dfrac{3}{4}.$
question.choice2: The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $w=\dfrac{v^2}{2}.$
question.choice3: The critical points lie on the $uw-$ plane.
question.choice4: The critical points lie on the plane $v=u.$
question.choice5: The critical points lie on the planes $v=\pm w .$
question.explanation:
For a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\w\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w)\\y(u,v,w)\\z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} & \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have

\[ x(u,v,w) = u+3w, \qquad y(u,v,w) = v+2w, \qquad z(u,v,w) = v^2-u. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &=1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= 0 & \quad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial w} &= 3 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 0 & \quad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial w} &= 2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} &= -1 & \quad \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} &= 2v & \quad \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} &= 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3\\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2v & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2v & 0 \end{vmatrix} + 3\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1& 2v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=1(0-4v) + 3(0+1)\\[5pt] &= 3-4v. \end{align*}

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} =0.$ So, we obtain

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} &= 0 \\[5pt] 3-4v &= 0. \end{align*}

The equation $3-4v = 0$ defines the plane $v=\dfrac{3}{4}.$
